https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/14/horv.text: Menü Kereső Horvátországi erdőtűz: már négy magyar sérültről tud a külügy Külföld Belföld A horvátországi Adria-parti nyaralóhely, Omiš környékén pusztító erdőtűzben leégett tengerparti bár 2026. augusztus 14-én – Fotó: Josko Ponos / AP / MTI Barnóczki Brigitta Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Négy magyar állampolgár sérüléséről kapott jelzést a Külügyminisztérium a horvátországi erdőtűzzel kapcsolatban, a Facebookon azt írták, jelenleg két magyar tartózkodik kórházban, őket várhatóan még ma hazaengedhetik. A külügy közvetlenül intézkedett a sérült magyarok segítségnyújtásáról. Az Omiš térségében, Horvátország magyarok által is kedvelt tengerparti szakaszán csütörtök este kialakult erdőtűz fejleményeiről azt írták, folyamatosan nyomon követik az erdőtűzben érintett magyarok helyzetét. A minisztérium azt írta, a Konzuli Tájékoztatási és Ügyeleti Központhoz 13 közvetlen megkeresés érkezett, sokan a tűz gyors terjedése miatt kénytelenek voltak elhagyni szálláshelyüket, és biztonságosabb területre menekülni. Egy sportcsarnokban lett a befogadóközpont Omišban, itt 45 magyart regisztráltak A külügy szerint a magyar állampolgárok biztonságban vannak, többen Splitben, Makarskában, Trogirban, illetve Omiš biztonságos területein tartózkodnak, a hajnalban segítséget kérők jelentős része pedig már úton van Magyarország felé saját autóval vagy tömegközlekedéssel, és további konzuli segítséget nem igényel. A hivatalos tájékoztatás szerint tíz magyar állampolgár esetében merülhet fel helyszíni transzfer biztosítása: két fő Splitből Omišba, nyolc pedig az omiši sportcsarnokból a szálláshelyére szeretne eljutni. A konzuli szolgálat folyamatos kapcsolatban áll a sportcsarnokban tartózkodó magyarokkal és a Splitben lévő magyarokkal is. Zadarból két magyar rendőr érkezett a konzuli munka segítésére, az omiši befogadóközpontban összesen 45 magyar állampolgárt regisztráltak. A minisztérium nem sokkal fél kettő előtt azt írta, hamarosan megérkezik a helyszínre a spliti magyar konzul is, és Zágrábból is úton van a külügy egyik munkatársa. Orbán Anita külügyminiszter korábban arról posztolt , hogy eddig legalább 58 magyar állampolgárt kellett kimenekíteni a súlyos horvátországi erdőtűz érintette területekről. Pelješac-félszigeten is erdőtűz pusztít Reggel írtunk arról, hogy csütörtök este súlyos erdőtűz alakult ki a horvát tengerparton, Dalmáciában, az Omištól délre fekvő Lokva Rogoznica térségében, a horvát hatóságok hivatalos tájékoztatása szerint a tűz lakóházakat és szálláshelyeket is veszélyeztet, ezért megkezdték a helyi lakosság és a turisták evakuálását. Az oltásban több mint 110 tűzoltó vesz részt, lezárták a D8-as főutat, az oltást pedig az erősödő szél és a gyorsan terjedő bozót- és fenyőerdőtűz is nehezíti. A Külügyminisztérium posztja szerint Omiš térségében jelenleg már nincsenek nyílt lángok, a tűzoltók és a bevetett Canadair repülőgépek az izzó gócok felszámolásán dolgoznak, de az éjszaka folyamán a térségből mintegy kétezer embert evakuáltak. Azt is írták, hogy közben Pelješac-félszigeten, Kuna Pelješka közelében is erdőtűz alakult ki, amely az erős szél miatt gyorsan terjed, a horvát hatóságok nagy erőkkel dolgoznak a megfékezésén. A magyar külügy arra kéri a kint tartózkodó magyarokat, hogy kövessék a helyi hatóságok utasításait, a Konzinfo aktuális tájékoztatásait, baj esetén pedig a Konzuli Szolgálat a nap 24 órájában elérhető. https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-w.text: In a throwaway comment this week, Donald Trump made clear that he does not regard the war in Ukraine as a conflict with fault on both sides. “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine,” the U.S. president said. “They have not been doing that much.” To residents of Kyiv — who have endured weeks of intensifying bombardment — and Ukraine’s allies across Europe, the remark confirmed a growing impression that the U.S. is taking Russia leader Vladimir Putin’s side in the war. “American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years,” the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday. The reason Ukraine hasn’t “surrendered on Putin’s terms” so far is because Europe has been providing so much support, she added. Advertisement Advertisement As they scratch their heads for explanations for Trump’s latest turn against Ukraine, some European officials and diplomats think it comes down to the president’s personal preferences, as much as his country’s political aims. “I do think it’s a personal thing,” said former British Cabinet minister David Lidington, now distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a leading security think tank in London. “Trump is self-centered — his personal predilections for dictators and autocrats, his desire to give opportunities to U.S. businesses … are very important parts of his motivation.” In private, EU officials agree. “Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. He just doesn’t like him,” said one government official who has observed both men closely. “That makes it harder to get the U.S. to help on peace. Everything is a rational business deal with Trump, until it’s not.” A diplomat from an EU country — granted anonymity, like others in this report, to discuss sensitive matters — said the inconsistent Trump could change his mind again and reverse recent moves against Ukraine. The U.S. president has chopped and changed on many issues, “except one thing,” the diplomat said. “He seems to be supportive of the Russians.” “He’s been critical of Ukraine, the EU, NATO, but hardly ever said anything critical about Putin. It is striking. We have to deal with an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else,” the diplomat said. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Advertisement Advertisement Mounting losses For Ukraine and its European allies, the idea that nothing can or will change Trump’s feelings about Zelenskyy is a bleak one. After four-and-a-half years of war, Kyiv is running low on funding, air defenses and — amid swelling support for Europe’s populist right — facing a potential loss of political support in the months ahead. Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff met the Ukrainian president and the leaders of Norway and Finland for talks in Oslo on Tuesday, and will head to St. Petersburg to discuss peace proposals with the Russian leadership on Wednesday as the White House pushes hard for a ceasefire. One option Putin will be offered is a three-way leaders’ summit with Trump and Zelenskyy. Previous efforts to get the Russian president to attend such a meeting have failed, however, and EU diplomats do not believe Putin is showing any genuine desire for a ceasefire. That is partly what makes Trump’s hostility toward Zelenskyy so problematic. “There is a clear consensus across Europe that Putin does not want peace,” a second EU diplomat said. “He will need to be forced into peace.” U.S. President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives for talks at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, on Aug. 15, 2025. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images But instead of making demands of Putin, Trump has ratcheted up his pressure on Zelenskyy, even amid escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities this month. Ukraine’s leader is feeling the strain, as he told his EU counterparts in private meetings in Brussels last week, according to the first diplomat. In a succession of highly critical comments in recent days, Trump has said Zelenskyy “doesn’t care” and “doesn’t want to end this war;” and should be replaced as leader or as Ukraine’s negotiator. “President Putin would like to see a settlement,” Trump said . “President Zelenskyy could have solved this war, or he could have made a deal, many times.” Advertisement Advertisement The Oval Office beating Trump’s animosity may date back to an incident during his first term in 2019, when he urged the Ukrainian leader to help with an investigation into Joe Biden, who eventually defeated Trump in the following presidential election, Lidington said. A succession of hostile encounters in the years since — including in the Oval Office in February 2025 — have reinforced the impression, he said. “It was clear that in the infamous meeting in the White House that Trump and [Vice President JD] Vance had planned that public beating-up of Zelenskyy and it struck me then that there was a strong personal element to this,” said Lidington. “I think there’s another element, which is that if you look at the people Trump tries to court, it tends to be autocratic strongman — and it is ‘man’ — leaders,” Lidington said. He recalled attending a dinner with world leaders in 2018 to mark the centenary of the end of World War I in Paris. French President Emmanuel Macron and the German chancellor at the time, Angela Merkel, were playing joint hosts “at the top table,” but Trump was not interested in making small talk with either of them, Lidington said. “It was pretty obvious from the body language that Trump was impatient with them and one of the people he really wanted to talk to was [Turkish leader Recep Tayyip] Erdoğan and other people who were a bit more in that strongman image that he likes to portray himself,” he observed. ‘Strange stories’ A senior official from a European country familiar with the Ukraine talks said Trump’s motives were partly political, partly about calculating what would be profitable and partly about personalities. Advertisement Advertisement “They are currently in an election cycle and need someone to blame for rising prices,” the official said. “In general, Trump tends to like various types of people and leaders. He actually has a fondness for successful and cheerful people.” In recent days, Zelenskyy has warned his country is suffering more civilian casualties because the U.S. has cut back on support, including Starlink and Starshield services that help Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks and plan operations. “We still have no explanation for this, just different strange stories,” Zelenskyy told U.S. congressmen on Monday. This month, the advanced warnings of incoming Russian missile attacks from U.S. partners have failed to come through as normal . Ukraine is also running low on Patriot missile interceptors, he said. The Pentagon has not issued an official comment on the Ukrainian complaints. The U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said 328 civilians were killed and more than 2,000 wounded across Ukraine last month, an 85% increase compared to September 2025. The U.N. said that the first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in Ukraine in years, driven by increased missile and drone strikes. The first EU diplomat quoted above said many European governments were irritated that Trump had cut them out of his conversations with Putin so far. “There is probably much more dialogue between the Americans and the Russians than we might know,” the diplomat said. Tuesday’s meeting with Witkoff in Norway raised the possibility that direct engagement with Putin might be back on the cards, for Zelenskyy at least. “Today was a good day for peace,” Finland’s President Alexander Stubb said after attending the talks in Oslo. “On a substantive and technical level we have actually made a lot of progress under the radar in the past week or so and now I feel that the process is back on track,” Stubb said. The process is now going in the right direction again, he added. “Hopefully, we don’t do any backtracking.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/07/dead.text: Drones have left a trail of destruction across the Black Sea, sinking commercial ships, setting vessels ablaze and killing civilians — exposing the challenge Europe faces in protecting one of its most vulnerable maritime regions.Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev described a drone attack on Tuesday, some 130km off the country's coast, as "absolutely unacceptable". One merchant ship sank and another was damaged. Radev did not attribute blame, with an investigation still underway.Romanian Foreign Minister Oana-Silvia Țoiu described a deadly incident off the country’s coast a day earlier as “a flagrant violation of international law”.On Monday, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying Ukrainian grain caught fire and subsequently sank off Romania. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the vessel had been attacked by Russian drones. Two people onboard were killed.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned both incidents."The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning," she said. "Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."The incidents have renewed scrutiny of Europe's ability to protect shipping and critical infrastructure in the Black Sea, more than a year after the EU launched a strategy to strengthen security in the region.When the Black Sea Security Strategy was unveiled in May 2025, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that the region was bearing the spillover effects of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine."The Black Sea region is the prime target for hybrid actions. The European Union aims to boost cooperation to combat cyberattacks, disinformation, and other hostile actions," she said.“Recurring airspace violations and attacks on ports and shipping lanes highlight this reality."The policy was aimed at ensuring the security of this maritime corridor, as well as protecting critical infrastructure and assets, such as offshore installations and subsea cables.It also promised the development of a Black Sea Maritime Security Hub aimed at coordinating support and boosting coast-guard cooperation, among other activities. The hub would also analyse seabed sensor data and alert allies to potential dangers and incoming threats.Asked to assess the effectiveness of the policy in light of this week’s recent incursions, European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said 65 projects worth €200 million had been initiated in the region because of the policy.“To add in that context, the European Maritime Safety Agency has offered its support to the Romanian and Bulgarian authorities, in line with its role in providing European-level maritime safety and situational awareness support,” he said.“Romania and Bulgaria requested satellite imagery to enhance situational awareness following the attacks, and we are currently delivering the shots.”On the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub, Wigand said it is a project led by Romania and Bulgaria that aims to “help enhance maritime situational awareness and reflection of critical infrastructure”.A European Commission report on the implementation of the EU’s Black Sea Strategy from July confirmed that the two countries had jointly developed a concept for the hub, which aims, among other initiatives, to counter complex hybrid threats.In the wake of Bulgaria’s incursion, Romania’s foreign minister said on Tuesday the hub will be located in both of the countries’ main ports, Constanța and Varna, respectively.But a leaked copy of the EU’s landmark Annual Defence Readiness report shows major shortfalls across Europe’s defence capabilities, particularly when it comes to maritime warfare.The document, prepared by the European Defence Agency with contributions from the Commission and the EU's foreign policy unit, the European External Action Service, assesses whether the 27 member states are on track to achieve defence readiness by 2030.Although EU governments plan to invest approximately €98.9 billion from 2024-2029 in maritime capabilities, current deficiencies affect a range of naval operations.“Critical gaps also remain in naval munitions and missile stockpiles, naval Integrated Air and Missile Defence (IAMD), long-range strike capabilities, and the protection of seabed infrastructure,” the report states.To fix the problem, the report recommends three courses of action: developing maritime domain awareness, balancing investment in large combat platforms with naval strike capabilities, and investing in supporting enablers such as seabed protection.Mihai Sebastian Chihaia, a maritime security expert at the European Policy Centre, said the Black Sea had received too little attention in Europe's wider defence debate and argued that strategies alone were insufficient.“We have quite a few strategies, we have quite a few directions, but to really secure the Black Sea, you actually need capabilities,” he told Euronews. These capabilities include intelligence-gathering operations, such as sensors and radars, for example.Chihaia argued that NATO — the cornerstone of European collective defence — could also develop a dedicated Black Sea strategy.In light of the drone incidents from earlier this week, Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey have stressed they are coordinating efforts to strengthen security in the region.But Chihaia said what remained missing was a broader vision for the Black Sea's future security architecture. Despite years of discussion, NATO has yet to produce one. "This hasn't happened," he said.Chihaia said the Commission's role is to provide directions and ideas for the member states. This may include funding options, such as the Security Action For Europe (SAFE) defence loan programme.“It’s really to incentivise the member states to work together, to develop new technological solutions, and to integrate them,” he said.Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Bulgaria and Romania "play a crucial role to defend our eastern flank", adding that the two countries are receiving a combined €20 billion under SAFE.
